title: Reset a Dead or Locked-Up Thermostat
mechanism_check: The thermostat is the low-voltage brain: it calls for heat, cool, or fan over the R/W/Y/G wires.
A blank screen usually means dead batteries or lost 24V power from the furnace or air handler.
A frozen display is crashed firmware; it never carries high voltage, so reseating it is safe.
improvised_tools: Phone camera to photograph wire terminals before touching anything
steps: Read the display: blank means power loss, frozen means crashed firmware.
Pop the cover and swap in fresh batteries, matching the + and - marks.
If still blank, check the furnace or air-handler breaker and any wall switch beside the furnace.
Frozen display: pull the thermostat body off its subbase, wait 60 seconds, re-seat it firmly.
Set the mode to cool or heat, move the setpoint a few degrees past room temperature, and listen for the equipment to answer.
stop_conditions: If you smell gas at the furnace, stop: leave the house and call the gas company from outside.
Do not open the furnace cabinet or touch wiring beyond the thermostat subbase.
If the thermostat smells of burning plastic, stop and kill its breaker.

title: Cut a Filter to Fit When the Right Size Is Missing
mechanism_check: The filter seals the return path so unfiltered air cannot bypass the indoor coil.
A gappy filter is worse than a slightly restrictive one: bypass dirt coats the coil permanently.
The airflow arrow must point toward the blower, never away from it.
improvised_tools: An oversized pleated filter (next size up)
Cardboard or foam scraps to fill gaps
steps: Measure the filter slot: length, width, and depth.
Buy the next size up from what the slot needs.
Cut the filter media along its cardboard frame to your measured size.
Reinforce the cut edge with painter's tape so fibers cannot shed into the airstream.
Fill any slot gaps with cardboard or foam so air cannot sneak around the filter.
Slide it in with the arrow pointing toward the blower, and write the install date on the frame.
stop_conditions: Never run the system with no filter at all.
If the filter will not seat flat without force, it is the wrong media: get the proper size.
If the filter slot is rusted through or the door will not close, stop and have a tech repair the rack.

title: Restore a Tripped Breaker or Blown Disconnect Safely
mechanism_check: The breaker protects the wire, not the equipment: a trip means something faulted.
Furnace and condenser each have their own disconnect; an outdoor pull-out disconnect may hold fuses.
A handle sitting in the middle position means tripped; it must go fully OFF before it can be reset.
improvised_tools: Notebook to record which breaker tripped and when
Phone to photograph the panel labels
steps: Identify which equipment is dead: indoor unit, outdoor unit, or both.
Find the tripped breaker: the handle sits between ON and OFF.
Inspect the condenser for debris, damage, or burning smell before resetting.
Push the breaker handle fully to OFF, then firmly to ON.
If there is an outdoor pull-out disconnect, pull the handle, check the fuses, and re-seat it.
If the breaker trips again immediately, leave it OFF and stop.
stop_conditions: Never keep resetting a breaker that trips twice: the fault is real, call an electrician or HVAC tech.
Do not open a fused disconnect without pulling the handle out first.
If the panel is hot, humming, or smells burnt, stop and call an electrician.

title: Walk the House: Register Airflow Audit
mechanism_check: Comfort follows airflow: the rooms that get air are the rooms that get comfortable.
Closed or furniture-blocked registers starve rooms; blocked returns starve the whole system.
Supply registers blow, return grilles suck: both must be open for the loop to work.
improvised_tools: Tissue paper or a ribbon on a stick
Masking tape to mark dead registers
steps: Set the system to FAN ON so air moves continuously during the audit.
Hold tissue at every supply register and every return grille.
Mark with tape any register with weak or no airflow.
Move furniture, rugs, and curtains off every blocked grille.
Open all supply registers at least halfway, including unused rooms.
Recheck the marked registers; the ones still dead feed the next entries.
stop_conditions: Do not enter an attic or crawlspace without a solid plank to walk on.
If a register has no airflow and the duct is crushed behind drywall, stop and call a tech.

title: Clear a Clogged Condensate Drain
mechanism_check: The indoor coil wrings water from the air; it leaves by gravity through a white PVC drain.
Algae grows in the trap and chokes it; the pan fills until the float switch kills the system.
No cooling with a full drain pan and a tripped float switch is a drain problem, not a refrigerant problem.
improvised_tools: Zip ties to secure the hose after
steps: Find the white PVC drain line leaving the indoor unit and its cleanout tee.
Hold the wet/dry vac hose tight over the outside end of the drain for two minutes.
Pour a cup of white vinegar into the cleanout tee to knock back algae.
Verify a steady drip or stream at the outside termination.
Check the drain pan: lift and release the float switch so it resets.
Run the system and confirm the pan stays dry.
stop_conditions: If the drain pan is overflowing into the ceiling, kill power to the unit and call a tech.
If the drain line is broken or disconnected inside a wall, stop: that is a repair, not a cleaning.
Never pour drain cleaner or bleach concentrate into the line: it can damage the coil pan.

title: Diagnose Thermostat Misbehavior: Ghost Calls and Short Cycles
mechanism_check: The thermostat controls to the air around it, not the air in your bedroom.
Sunlight, drafts, and nearby heat sources lie to the sensor and cause ghost calls.
Cycle-rate or anticipator settings tune run length; weak batteries cause relay chatter.
improvised_tools: Phone as a thermometer for comparison
Masking tape to mark the original setting
steps: Write down the symptom pattern: short cycles, overruns, or calls with no one home.
Check placement: sun on the unit, a draft from a door, or a lamp or TV underneath it.
Swap in fresh batteries even if the display looks alive.
Level the unit on the wall; an unlevel mechanical thermostat misreads.
Adjust the cycle-rate setting one notch toward longer cycles and watch one full cycle.
If behavior is unchanged after a day, the thermostat or its wire may be failing.
stop_conditions: If you smell gas at the furnace, stop: leave the house and call the gas company.
Do not disconnect thermostat wires unless the furnace breaker is OFF and verified.
If the subbase is scorched, stop and kill its breaker.

title: AC Not Cooling: Airflow-First Diagnosis Without Gauges
mechanism_check: Most no-cool calls are airflow, power, or a dirty condenser, not refrigerant.
Delta-T, the temperature drop between return and supply, should be 15 to 20 F on a healthy system.
Gauges and the sealed refrigerant system are the licensed-tech line: diagnose up to it, never past it.
steps: Confirm the thermostat is calling for cool and the indoor blower is running.
Check the filter and all registers per hvac-002 and hvac-004.
Measure delta-T: thermometer at a return grille and at a nearby supply; compare.
Look at the indoor coil through the access panel for frost or heavy dirt.
Check the outdoor unit: fan spinning, no debris packed in the fins.
Hose the condenser coil from inside out with the disconnect OFF, then restore power and re-measure delta-T.
stop_conditions: If the compressor runs, coils are clean, airflow is good, and there is still no cooling, stop: suspect refrigerant and call a licensed tech.
Never attach gauges or piercing valves: refrigerant handling is licensed-only by law.
De-energize and verify before touching any electrical compartment.

title: Thaw a Frozen Evaporator Coil and Hunt the Cause
mechanism_check: Ice forms when airflow drops or refrigerant runs low: both starve the coil of heat.
Running a frozen system slugs the compressor with liquid and can kill it.
The safe thaw is time plus moving air: set the system to OFF with FAN ON.
improvised_tools: Towels and buckets for melt water
steps: Turn the system to OFF and the fan to ON; let the coil thaw for several hours.
Never chip, scrape, or heat the ice: you will puncture the coil.
Once fully thawed and dry, check the filter, the blower wheel, and that every register is open.
Restart cooling and watch for an hour: strong cold air means airflow was the cause.
If it refreezes within a day with clean airflow, low refrigerant is likely.
stop_conditions: Never chip at ice on the coil: a punctured coil is a full replacement.
If it refreezes after the airflow check, stop and call a licensed tech: refrigerant work is licensed-only.
If the compressor makes grinding or knocking sounds, kill power and call a tech.

title: Furnace Won't Light: Pilot and Igniter Diagnosis
mechanism_check: The board runs a fixed script: inducer runs, pressure switch proves, igniter glows, gas valve opens, flame sensor proves.
The first stage that fails to complete is the fault zone; everything after it is a guess.
The gas valve must be open and the furnace breaker on before any of this means anything.
improvised_tools: Phone to record the startup sequence for playback
steps: Call for heat and watch the full sequence through the sight glass; do not open the burner door while it fires.
Note exactly where it stalls: no inducer sound, inducer runs but no glow, glow but no flame, flame then lockout.
Verify the gas valve handle is parallel to the pipe and the furnace breaker is on.
If the igniter never glows, suspect the igniter or the board.
If it glows but no flame appears, suspect the gas valve or pressure switch.
Flame that lights then drops out points at the flame sensor: see hvac-010.
stop_conditions: Any gas smell at any point: stop, leave the house, call the gas company from outside.
Never bypass a safety switch: rollout, pressure, or limit switches are there to prevent fires.
Gas valve, pressure switch, and board replacement are licensed-tech work.

title: Clean a Dirty Flame Sensor
mechanism_check: The flame sensor proves flame by conducting a tiny current through the flame to ground.
Carbon coating insulates the rod, the board sees no flame, and it locks the furnace out.
This is the most common fixable cause of flame-then-lockout, and it is homeowner-grade.
improvised_tools: Fine emery cloth or steel wool
steps: Kill power at the furnace switch and verify the blower is dead.
Open the burner compartment and find the single-wire metal rod sitting in front of a burner.
Remove its mounting screw and slide the rod out, noting its position.
Polish the rod gently with emery cloth until the metal shines; do not bend it.
Reinstall it exactly as found, restore power, and watch one full ignition cycle.
stop_conditions: Any gas smell: stop, leave the house, call the gas company from outside.
If the rod is cracked or the porcelain is broken, stop: replacement is a tech part swap.
If cleaning does not fix the lockout, stop and call a tech: the board or gas valve may be at fault.

title: Diagnose a Failing Blower Capacitor by Sound and Spin
mechanism_check: The run capacitor gives the motor its starting phase shift; without it the motor just hums.
A dying capacitor shows as slow starts, humming with no spin, or intermittent running.
Capacitors store a lethal charge after power is cut: this entry is diagnose-only, never touch.
improvised_tools: A wooden dowel or stick to spin the wheel with power OFF
steps: Call for FAN ON and listen at the blower compartment: a loud hum with no rotation points at the capacitor.
Kill power, open the compartment, and look at the capacitor case: a bulged or leaking case is a failed capacitor.
With power OFF, spin the blower wheel by hand with the stick: it should turn freely.
If it turns freely by hand but will not start on its own, the capacitor is the prime suspect.
Close it up and call a tech with the symptom list: hum, free spin, no start.
stop_conditions: Never touch capacitor terminals: they hold a lethal charge even with power off.
Capacitor replacement, including safe discharge and wiring, is tech work.
If the wheel will not turn by hand, the motor or bearing is seized: stop and call a tech.

title: Quiet a Noisy Blower: Diagnose the Rattle
mechanism_check: Blower noise comes from a short list: loose wheel, rubbing housing, debris, worn bearings, or duct vibration.
The set screw on the blower wheel loosens over years and lets the wheel walk and rub.
Bearing noise is a grind that gets worse with speed; rubbing is a scrape at one point in each rotation.
improvised_tools: Rubber pads or folded cardboard for shims
steps: Kill power at the furnace switch and verify the blower is dead.
Open the blower compartment and look for debris, a loose wheel, or scrape marks on the housing.
Spin the wheel by hand: feel for wobble, and tighten the set screw on the flat of the motor shaft.
Check that the motor mounts are snug and the wheel clears the housing all the way around.
Pad any duct takeoff that rattles against the cabinet, restore power, and listen through one full cycle.
stop_conditions: Bearing grind that does not change with cleaning and tightening means motor replacement: call a tech.
If the blower wheel is cracked or a blade is bent, stop: it is unbalanced and unsafe to run.
De-energize and verify before putting hands anywhere near the wheel.

title: Seal Leaking Duct Joints Without Mastic
mechanism_check: Ducts leak at the joints, not in the middle of the run.
The seal must flex with temperature swings: aluminum foil tape flexes, cloth duct tape dries and fails.
Zip ties over the tape at round joints act as a permanent clamp.
improvised_tools: Aluminum foil tape, not cloth duct tape
Old blankets for wrapping exposed runs
steps: Run the system and feel along every accessible joint for blowing air.
Wipe each leaky joint clean so the tape can bond.
Wrap foil tape around the joint with a two-inch overlap on each side.
Cinch a zip tie over the tape at round joints as a clamp.
Wrap exposed runs with blanket material and tape the seams.
Recheck with the system running: sealed joints should feel dead still.
stop_conditions: Do not disturb old duct wrap that looks fibrous and gray, pre-1990: it may contain asbestos. Stop and get it tested.
Do not apply sealant inside the airstream near the furnace heat exchanger.
If a joint is rusted through or crushed, tape is not enough: call a tech.

title: Install and Seal a Window Air Conditioner
mechanism_check: The unit must tilt slightly outward so condensate drains outside, not into the wall.
The seal between unit and window is the insulation layer: side gaps are where the cooling escapes.
The accordion side panels are the weakest seal and the first place to upgrade.
steps: Set the unit in the window with a slight outward tilt, about a quarter inch, and check with the level.
Screw L-brackets into the top sash so the window cannot be lifted from outside.
Replace or back the accordion side panels with cut foam board for a real seal.
Tape every seam between unit, panels, and window frame.
Seal the gap between the upper and lower sash where they meet.
Plug the unit directly into a wall outlet, never an extension cord, and verify condensate drips outside.
stop_conditions: If the breaker trips when the compressor starts, stop: the circuit is undersized. Call an electrician for a dedicated circuit.
Second-floor installs must be bracketed to structure, not balanced on the sill.
Never run the unit with the tilt inward: water will rot the sill and wall.

title: Wash a Dirty Outdoor Condenser Coil
mechanism_check: The condenser rejects indoor heat through its fins; a dirt blanket on the fins strangles heat rejection.
Water from the inside out pushes dirt off instead of packing it deeper.
Bent fins block airflow the same as dirt does.
improvised_tools: Garden hose with a spray nozzle
A butter knife as a fin comb
Screwdriver to remove the top grille
steps: Pull the outdoor disconnect to kill power to the condenser and verify the fan is dead.
Remove the top grille, noting where each wire and screw goes.
Hose the fins from the inside out, top to bottom, until the water runs clear.
Straighten bent fins gently with the butter knife, working with the fin direction.
Clear leaves and sludge from the base pan so water can drain.
Reassemble, restore power, and confirm the fan runs and discharge air feels warm.
stop_conditions: If the fins are oily or you see oil stains on the pad, stop: that signals a refrigerant leak. Call a licensed tech.
Never use a pressure washer on the coil: it folds the fins flat.
De-energize and verify before removing any grille or panel.

title: Clear Condenser Airflow: Vegetation and Debris
mechanism_check: The condenser needs two feet of clearance on all sides and five feet above for its discharge.
Vegetation against the unit recirculates hot discharge air back into the coil.
Mulch piled against the base holds moisture and rots the cabinet.
steps: Cut all vegetation back two feet from the unit on every side.
Rake leaves, grass, and trash out from around and under the unit.
Pull mulch and soil back from the base so the cabinet edge is exposed.
Check that the unit sits level on its pad.
Make sure no dryer vent or exhaust blows lint or heat directly at the coil.
stop_conditions: If the unit has sunk and the refrigerant lines are pulled taut, stop: call a tech before attempting to level it.
Do not dig around buried refrigerant or electrical lines with tools.

title: Furnace Eyeball Inspection: Flame Color and Rollout
mechanism_check: A clean gas flame is blue with steady cones; yellow, lazy flames mean incomplete combustion.
Incomplete combustion makes carbon monoxide and soot.
The rollout switch trips when flame escapes the heat exchanger: a tripped rollout is a red flag, never a nuisance.
improvised_tools: Phone camera to document what you see
steps: Call for heat and watch the flames through the sight glass; never open the burner door while it fires.
Healthy flames are steady and blue; note any yellow tipping or lazy floating flames.
Look for soot stains around the burner door or on the sight glass.
Note whether the rollout switch has tripped; if it has, do not reset it more than once.
Yellow flames plus soot means schedule a burner cleaning; a tripped rollout means call a tech now.
stop_conditions: A tripped rollout switch with soot present: stop, kill the gas, and call a licensed tech.
Any carbon monoxide alarm: evacuate immediately and call emergency services.
Never reset a rollout switch repeatedly to keep the heat running.

title: Diagnose Short Cycling
mechanism_check: Short cycling is runs under five minutes with rapid restarts: it wears equipment and never dehumidifies.
Common causes: thermostat placement, dirty filter, blocked condenser, oversized unit, or a tripping high-limit switch.
Two to three cycles per hour with ten-minute-plus runs is normal.
steps: Time the on and off periods for thirty minutes and count cycles per hour.
Rule out the thermostat first per hvac-006: drafts, sun, and heat sources.
Check the filter and condenser airflow per hvac-002 and hvac-016.
If the furnace runs three to five minutes then stops on limit, suspect restricted airflow or overheating.
If the AC short cycles with clean airflow, suspect low refrigerant or an oversized unit.
stop_conditions: A furnace repeatedly tripping its high-limit switch is an overheating risk: stop and call a tech.
Short cycling with any suspicion of refrigerant issues goes to a licensed tech.
Never bypass a limit switch to keep the system running.

title: Balance Hot and Cold Rooms with Improvised Dampers
mechanism_check: Air takes the easiest path: near rooms steal airflow from far rooms.
Partially closing strong rooms pushes air to weak rooms; the system tolerates this in small doses.
Never close more than about a third of total supply: the blower and coil need their airflow.
steps: Run the airflow audit from hvac-004 and rank rooms strongest to weakest.
Partially cover the registers in the two or three strongest rooms, starting at half closed.
Re-measure the weak rooms with tissue and adjust in small steps.
Mark the final positions with tape so they can be restored.
Recheck after a day of normal use, and again when the season changes.
stop_conditions: If duct noise rises sharply or the indoor coil starts frosting, open everything back up: static pressure is too high.
Freezing coil or screaming ducts means undo the changes immediately and call a tech for a real balance.
Never fully seal supply registers in a room with a gas appliance.

title: Diagnose a Failed Condensate Pump
mechanism_check: Where gravity cannot drain the coil, a small pump lifts the condensate to a drain.
A float in the reservoir triggers the pump; a second safety float kills the system on high water.
No cooling with a full pump reservoir is a pump problem until proven otherwise.
steps: Confirm the pump's outlet has power and the pump is plugged in.
Pour water into the reservoir and listen: the pump should kick on and empty it.
Check the discharge hose for kinks, sags, or disconnections.
Clean sludge from the reservoir and the float so it moves freely.
Lift the safety float by hand: the system should shut off, proving the safety works.
stop_conditions: If water is near electrical components, kill power to the unit before touching anything.
If the pump is hardwired rather than plug-in, replacement wiring is electrician or tech work.
A pump that runs but moves no water may have a failed check valve: replace the unit.

title: Repair Crushed Attic Flex Duct
mechanism_check: Flex duct is a wire helix under a plastic liner: when crushed, the liner kinks and halves the airflow.
The fix is mechanical: pull it straight and support it so it cannot sag back.
Supports must cradle the duct, never pinch it.
improvised_tools: Mule tape, old belts, or rope for hangers
steps: De-energize the air handler and verify it is dead before entering the work area.
Find the crushed or sagging section by following the run from the plenum.
Pull the run straight, working the kinks out of the inner liner by hand.
Hang the run every four feet with wide straps so it cannot sag between supports.
Tape any torn outer jacket with foil tape to protect the insulation.
Restore power and verify strong airflow at the register the run feeds.
stop_conditions: Attic work only from joists or a solid plank: falling through the ceiling is the real hazard here.
If the inner liner is torn open, the run needs replacement: call a tech.
Do not compress the duct to make a hanger fit: pinched duct is crushed duct.

title: Diagnose Return-Air Starvation
mechanism_check: The blower can only deliver what the return feeds it: a choked return chokes every supply.
Closed bedroom doors with no return path pressurize the room and starve the system.
Return grille area should roughly match total supply area.
steps: With the system running, close a bedroom door and feel the supply airflow: if it drops, the room lacks a return path.
Crack doors an inch or wedge them during system operation as an immediate test.
Check that every return grille is open and uncovered by furniture.
Verify the filter is not collapsed or sucked into the rack.
For a lasting fix, add a transfer grille over the door or a jumper duct: plan it, then have a tech install it.
stop_conditions: If the return duct is disconnected in the attic or crawlspace, stop and repair it per hvac-013 and hvac-021 before running the system.
Do not run the system with the filter rack open to the attic: it will pull in unconditioned air and contaminants.

title: Relight a Standing Pilot Safely
mechanism_check: The thermocouple holds the gas valve open once the pilot heats it; when it cools, gas flow stops.
Relighting follows the sequence printed on the gas valve: OFF, wait, PILOT, hold, ON.
The five-minute wait lets any unburned gas clear before you introduce a flame.
steps: Turn the gas valve to OFF and wait five full minutes.
Set the valve to PILOT and press and hold the button or knob.
Light the pilot with the long lighter while holding the button.
Keep holding for sixty seconds after it lights, then release slowly.
If the pilot stays lit, turn the valve to ON; if it drops out, repeat once.
Two failed attempts means a bad thermocouple or valve: stop and call a tech.
stop_conditions: Any gas smell beyond the brief puff while lighting: turn to OFF, leave the house, call the gas company from outside.
More than two failed attempts: stop. Do not keep trying.
Never bypass the thermocouple or hold the valve open manually.

title: Diagnose a Dead Hot-Surface Igniter
mechanism_check: The hot-surface igniter is fragile silicon-carbide ceramic that glows white-hot to light the burners.
A crack in the element is an open circuit: no glow, no ignition.
Skin oils contaminate the element and shorten its life: handle by the ceramic base only.
steps: Kill power at the furnace switch and verify the blower is dead.
Open the burner compartment and find the gray fork-shaped element in front of the burners.
Inspect it for white cracks or a broken tip: any crack means it is dead.
Note the part number and connector type, then close the compartment.
Order the exact replacement; never substitute a different wattage or shape.
stop_conditions: Any gas smell: stop, leave the house, call the gas company from outside.
Never touch the gray element with bare fingers, powered or not.
If the replacement connector does not match the board, stop: wiring it wrong destroys the board. Call a tech.

title: Replace a Blower Belt on a Belt-Drive Unit
mechanism_check: The motor drives the blower wheel through a V-belt; a thrown or glazed belt means no airflow.
Correct tension is about half an inch of deflection midway between pulleys.
Misaligned pulleys throw belts: the pulleys must sit in the same plane.
improvised_tools: Replacement belt matched to the old belt number
steps: Disconnect power to the unit and verify it is dead.
Remove the belt guard and note the exact belt routing before touching it.
Loosen the motor mount and slide the motor to release tension.
Fit the new belt, then slide the motor back to set half an inch of deflection.
Check pulley alignment with the straightedge and tighten everything.
Replace the guard, restore power, and watch the belt track centered for a full minute.
stop_conditions: If the blower shaft bearing is seized or the wheel wobbles on the shaft, stop: that is a tech rebuild.
If the belt threw because of misalignment you cannot correct, call a tech.
Never run the unit with the belt guard off.

title: Measure Static Pressure with an Improvised Manometer
mechanism_check: Total external static pressure tells you whether the duct system is strangling the blower.
A U-tube manometer reads inches of water column: the height difference between the legs is the pressure.
Most residential equipment is rated for 0.5 inches max; double that means the ducts are the problem.
improvised_tools: Drill with 3/8 inch bit and plastic plugs for test ports
steps: Form the tubing into a U, fill it halfway with colored water, and mount it beside a ruler.
With the system off, drill test ports in plain duct before and after the air handler; plug them when done.
Run the system and read each leg against the ruler: the difference is the pressure at that port.
Add the return-side and supply-side readings for total external static pressure.
Compare to the rating plate: high return-side means filter or return restriction, high supply-side means undersized ducts.
stop_conditions: Drill test ports in plain duct only: never into the heat exchanger, coil, or cabinet.
If total static is double the rating, stop adjusting and call a tech for duct remediation.
Seal every test port with a proper plug when finished: open holes leak.

title: Isolate Equipment Vibration and Duct Rumble
mechanism_check: Vibration travels through rigid contact: rubber or cork breaks the transmission path.
The unit must stay level while you pad it, or you trade noise for drainage and belt problems.
Duct rumble is usually a takeoff or hanger touching structure, not the equipment itself.
steps: With the system running, touch-test to find what is buzzing: pipes, ducts, the cabinet, or the wall.
Kill power, then slip rubber or cork pads under every rigid contact point.
Replace rigid duct hangers screwed to joists with strap hangers that let the duct float.
Verify the unit is still level after padding.
Restore power and listen: chase any remaining rumble to its contact point and pad it.
stop_conditions: If the compressor itself is shaking violently, kill power and stop: call a licensed tech.
Do not pad the unit so far out of level that condensate cannot drain.
If vibration started suddenly with a new noise, stop and inspect for a loose or broken mount before padding over it.

title: Deep-Clean a Mini-Split Indoor Unit
mechanism_check: A mini-split recirculates room air through a washable filter and a finned coil.
Dirty filters mean weak airflow and the musty smell of a dirty coil.
The filters must be fully dry before reinstalling or they grow mold inside the unit.
steps: Kill power at the mini-split disconnect and verify the unit is dead.
Open the front panel and slide out the filters.
Vacuum both sides, wash with mild soap and water, and air-dry completely.
Wipe the coil fins gently downward with a damp cloth; never bend the fins.
Wipe the blower wheel slots to remove dust buildup.
Reinstall the dry filters, close the panel, and restore power.
stop_conditions: Never spray water into the electrical section of the unit.
If the coil is iced over or the unit drips inside after cleaning, stop and call a tech.
If the filters are torn, replace them: running without them dirties the coil permanently.

title: Seal a Portable AC Exhaust Hose
mechanism_check: A single-hose portable fights itself: it exhausts room air and pulls hot makeup air in.
Hot air leaking back around the window kit and heat radiating off the hose erase the cooling.
The shorter and better-insulated the hose, the less the unit fights itself.
improvised_tools: Reflective blanket or car sunshade for a hose sleeve
steps: Tape every seam of the window-kit panel so no outside air slips around it.
Seal the gap between the kit and the window sash with foam tape.
Shorten the exhaust hose as much as the layout allows; every extra foot radiates heat.
Wrap the hose in the reflective sleeve and tape it closed.
Keep the unit off carpet so the condensate pan and drain stay accessible.
stop_conditions: If the unit repeatedly trips its breaker, stop: it is a 12-amp-plus load on a shared circuit. Call an electrician for a dedicated circuit.
Never extend the exhaust hose beyond the manufacturer's length.
If the unit leaks water onto the floor, stop and clear the drain before running it again.

title: Pair a Dehumidifier with AC as a Humidity Assist
mechanism_check: Half of uncomfortable is humidity: dry 78 F air feels better than humid 74 F air.
A dehumidifier lets the thermostat sit two to three degrees higher for the same comfort.
The dehumidifier adds heat as it runs, so placement away from the thermostat matters.
improvised_tools: Hygrometer, or a phone weather app as a rough proxy
Drain hose to a sink or floor drain
steps: Measure room humidity: above 60 percent relative humidity is the discomfort zone.
Set the dehumidifier in the dampest zone with its drain routed to a sink or drain.
Raise the AC setpoint two degrees and let the pair work for a day.
Check comfort and humidity: target 45 to 55 percent.
If humidity stays above 60 percent with both running, the AC coil may be underperforming.
stop_conditions: If the dehumidifier coils frost over repeatedly, unplug it: the unit is failing.
Never let the dehumidifier drain onto a floor with no drain: overflow ruins flooring.
Persistent high humidity with a clean system means call a tech to check the AC.

title: Start Up and Re-Pad an Evaporative Cooler
mechanism_check: A swamp cooler cools by evaporating water through its pads: dry pads mean hot air.
Mineral scale cakes the pads over a season and chokes evaporation.
The pump must wet every pad evenly before the blower starts, or dry spots blow hot.
improvised_tools: Replacement pads, aspen or rigid media
steps: Kill power to the cooler and verify it is dead.
Open the side panels and pull the old pads.
Scrub the reservoir and clean the pump screen of scale and debris.
Fit the new pads snug with no gaps at the edges.
Fill the reservoir, run the pump only, and verify every pad wets evenly.
Start the blower and crack a window on the far side of the house for exhaust air.
stop_conditions: Evaporative cooling only works in dry climates: if indoor humidity climbs past comfort, stop using it.
If the pump or motor is hardwired, replacement wiring is electrician or tech work.
Never run the blower with dry pads: it just blows hot dusty air.

title: Read a Gas Furnace Sequence of Operation to Fault-Find
mechanism_check: The board runs a fixed script: call for heat, inducer, pressure switch proves, igniter, gas valve, flame proved, blower on.
The LED blink code on the board names the failure; the legend is printed on the blower door.
The first stage that does not complete is the fault zone: everything past it is a guess.
improvised_tools: Phone to film the LED blink code
Furnace manual, or a photo of the model number to look it up
steps: Call for heat and watch the sequence, filming the LED through the sight glass.
Match the blink code to the legend on the blower door.
Walk the sequence in order and mark the first stage that does not complete.
Fix only what is homeowner-grade: filter, power, thermostat, flame sensor, condensate.
Write down the stage and the code, and hand that to the tech: it saves a diagnostic hour.
stop_conditions: Everything past the igniter and flame sensor: gas valve, pressure switch, control board, and heat exchanger are licensed-tech territory.
Any gas smell: stop, leave the house, call the gas company from outside.
Never clear a fault code and walk away: the code is evidence, not the problem.

title: Heat Pump on Aux Heat: Triage the Defrost and Backup
mechanism_check: Heat pumps ice up outdoors in winter and defrost themselves on a timer or sensor.
Below about 30 to 35 F the electric backup strips carry the load: constant AUX is expensive.
AUX stuck on with mild weather means the defrost cycle is failing, not that it is just cold.
steps: Check the outdoor unit: a light frost that clears is normal, heavy ice that never clears is not.
Verify the outdoor fan runs and the unit is not buried in snow or debris.
Note whether AUX or emergency heat is on constantly, and at what outdoor temperature.
As a stopgap, switch to emergency heat to stay warm while you arrange service.
If the unit never enters defrost, suspect the defrost sensor or board: call a tech.
stop_conditions: If the outdoor unit is iced solid and the reversing valve hisses constantly, stop and call a tech.
Refrigerant-side work on a heat pump is licensed-only by law.
Do not chip ice off the outdoor coil: you will damage the fins and tubing.

title: Relocate a Thermostat That Reads a Lie
mechanism_check: The thermostat controls to the air around it: a hallway by the kitchen is not the house.
The truth spot is an interior wall, about five feet high, away from vents, sun, and drafts.
Low-voltage thermostat wire is safe to handle only with the furnace power killed and verified.
improvised_tools: Fish tape or a straightened coat hanger
steps: Kill furnace power at the breaker and the furnace switch, and verify it is dead.
Photograph the existing wiring and label every wire by terminal letter.
Choose the new spot: interior wall, five feet high, no direct sun, draft, or supply vent.
Fish the wire through the wall to the new location and mount the subbase level.
Reconnect wire for wire to the labeled terminals.
Restore power and test both a heat call and a cool call end to end.
stop_conditions: If the existing wire is stapled inside the wall and will not pull, stop: fishing new cable through finished walls is tech or electrician work.
Never work low-voltage wiring with the furnace powered.
If any wire is nicked or bare beyond its terminal, stop and call a tech.

title: Design an Attic Duct Reroute on Paper
mechanism_check: Ducts lose capacity to length, elbows, and kinks: every bend costs airflow.
A trunk-and-branch layout with short straight branches beats a long snaking run.
A paper plan with CFM targets per room is what a licensed tech quotes from.
improvised_tools: The audit data from hvac-004 and hvac-026
steps: Map every register and its measured airflow from hvac-004.
Sketch a straight trunk with short branches, minimizing elbows and length.
Size each branch to its room load, roughly one CFM per square foot as a planning figure.
Note the insulation R-value the new runs need for the attic climate.
Check the plan against the static pressure budget from hvac-026.
Hand the finished plan to a licensed tech for execution and quoting.
stop_conditions: This entry is design-only: cutting and connecting ductwork is licensed-tech work.
Never touch refrigerant lines or the sealed system while planning or measuring.
Do not implement the reroute yourself: improper ductwork voids equipment warranties.

title: Zone a House with Improvised Register Baffles
mechanism_check: True zoning uses motorized dampers; the improvised version uses seasonal baffle positions.
The guardrail is static pressure: too much restriction freezes the coil or trips the furnace limit.
Delta-T at the coil must stay in the 15 to 20 F band while baffles are set.
steps: Define day and night zones: bedrooms versus living areas.
Set baffles to favor the occupied zone, starting with small adjustments.
Re-measure delta-T at the coil: it must stay between 15 and 20 F.
Walk the house and confirm every zone still gets some airflow.
Log the seasonal baffle positions so they can be repeated and reversed.
stop_conditions: Freezing coil, screaming ducts, or a tripping furnace limit: open everything back up immediately.
If the guardrails keep tripping, stop and call a tech for real motorized zoning.
Never fully seal supply registers in a room with a gas appliance.

title: Refrigerant-Leak Suspicion: Diagnose to the Line and Stop
mechanism_check: Low charge symptoms: ice on the suction line, hissing at the coil, warm supply air with a clean coil and good airflow, oily residue at joints.
These symptoms only count after airflow causes are ruled out per hvac-007 and hvac-008.
Confirmation, leak repair, and charging are licensed-only by law: this entry ends at the line.
improvised_tools: Eyes and ears only: no gauges, no piercing valves
steps: Rule out every airflow cause first: filter, blower, registers, condenser coil.
Look for oil stains at refrigerant line joints, the service valves, and the indoor coil.
Listen for hissing at the coil and lines with the system off.
Photograph anything suspicious: oil, ice patterns, damaged insulation.
Call a licensed tech and hand over the symptom list and photos: report, do not touch.
stop_conditions: HARD STOP: refrigerant handling, leak repair, charging, and opening the sealed system are licensed-technician-only by law.
Never attach gauges or piercing valves to the system.
If oil is actively spraying or you hear a loud hiss, kill power and call a tech immediately.

title: Teach the Why on a Live Call: Mentor an Apprentice
mechanism_check: An apprentice who only watches learns hands, not judgment; judgment transfers only through narration of reasoning.
Live calls are the training window: the apprentice remembers what they saw linked to a real house, not a bench demo.
Mentoring also pressure-tests your own diagnosis: explaining it out loud exposes sloppy reasoning.
improvised_tools: One real service call, even a simple one
The apprentice's hands, the mentor's voice
A rule: apprentice states the hypothesis before the mentor confirms
steps: Narrate the airflow-first sequence aloud as you walk: filter, return, supply, condenser.
Ask the apprentice to call the next test before you do it; correct the reasoning, not the person.
Hand them the one low-risk task you already planned: filter check, register walk, drain flush.
Let them state the diagnosis to you before you touch a tool; if it fails, walk the failure together.
End the call with one named lesson: one sentence the apprentice repeats back.
stop_conditions: If the apprentice is unsure near a gas line or electrical compartment, they stop and hand back to you.
Never let the apprentice open refrigerant work or gas valve areas: diagnose-only zones stay supervised.
If mentoring is slowing the call into a customer complaint, switch to silent watch and debrief later.

title: Write the Hypothesis Down Before You Touch a Tool
mechanism_check: Technicians who touch tools before thinking chase symptoms; the first hypothesis anchors every test that follows.
A written hypothesis turns a vague call into a pass/fail experiment: each measurement rules something out.
This is the core diagnostics discipline that separates callbacks from one-visit fixes.
improvised_tools: A pocket notebook or phone note
The call ticket: complaint in the customer's words
One pen line per hypothesis: symptom, cause, test, expected result
steps: Copy the customer's complaint verbatim; do not translate it into parts yet.
Write one hypothesis in cause-and-effect form: 'frozen coil because filter choked airflow.'
Write the single cheapest test that would kill that hypothesis.
Run the test, write the result, then write the next hypothesis or the fix.
On fix, record what you found and what ruled out the alternatives; read it before leaving.
stop_conditions: If two hypotheses both survive your tests, stop and call a second tech or licensed specialist rather than guessing.
If the next test requires opening the sealed refrigerant system, stop at the licensed-tech line.
If gas or burning smell appears mid-diagnosis, evacuate first and document later.

title: Run a Shoulder-Season Readiness Sweep
mechanism_check: Most failures are found cheapest in the shoulder season, when parts and tech time are plentiful and demand is low.
A readiness sweep converts reactive summer breakdowns into scheduled spring fixes: you control the calendar instead of the heat wave controlling you.
Customers who get a written readiness report call you first when something breaks: the sweep is marketing that fixes things.
improvised_tools: A one-page checklist: filter, coil, drain, capacitor look, airflow walk, thermostat
A template readiness letter with findings and recommended actions
Calendar reminders set for the next shoulder season
steps: Schedule the sweep in spring and fall, before the weather turns: own the slow weeks.
Run the same sequence every time: thermostat, filter, airflow walk, drain, condenser coil, outdoor clearance, furnace eyeball in fall.
Write findings plainly: what is fine, what will fail soon, what needs a licensed tech now.
Hand the customer the letter and price the soon-to-fail items while demand is low.
Log the sweep date; call back next season before the weather does.
stop_conditions: Anything past the licensed line (refrigerant, gas valve internals, heat exchanger cracks) goes in the letter as 'call a licensed tech,' never as a DIY fix.
If the furnace shows flame rollout or rusted-through cabinets, stop the sweep and flag it urgent.
Do not sell parts the house does not need: the letter's honesty is the marketing.

title: Run a Service Call So It Stays Profitable
mechanism_check: A service call is won or lost on the callback: one free return visit erases the margin of the paid one.
Diagnosis discipline (hvac-039) is the profit engine: right part first time beats fast part wrong time.
Quoted price protects trust; discovering extra work mid-call without a fresh quote destroys it.
improvised_tools: A flat-rate mental price list for common fixes: capacitor, contactor, drain clear, thermostat swap
The written hypothesis from hvac-039 as your receipt of competence
An exit walkdown habit: the five minutes that prevent the callback
steps: Arrive with the price before you start: state the diagnostic fee and what common fixes cost.
Diagnose fully before quoting parts; never quote from the doorway.
If you find a second problem mid-call, stop and quote it separately before touching it.
Fix, then run the full verification: the system must prove itself running before you pack up.
Do the exit walkdown: filters, registers, drain, thermostat set back where the customer wants it.
stop_conditions: If the fix crosses the licensed line, quote the referral, not the attempt: attempting it is liability, not profit.
If the customer pressures you to skip the safety check to save money, decline: your license and their house are the stake.
If you cannot verify the fix running, you have not finished: do not leave the call as 'fixed.'

title: Kill Callbacks with the Five-Minute Exit Walkdown
mechanism_check: Callbacks are rarely wrong diagnoses; they are forgotten steps: a filter left out, a drain left wet, a thermostat left in the wrong mode.
The exit walkdown is a fixed sequence that catches the forgets while you are still in the driveway.
Each prevented callback protects margin and reputation: the cheapest visit is the one you never make.
improvised_tools: A fixed five-point exit order, same every call
Your phone camera: one photo of the finished work
The customer's eyes: walk them through what changed
steps: Filter: installed, arrow correct, door closed and latched.
Thermostat: set back to the customer's setting and mode; confirm the equipment answers.
Drain and electrical: no water where it should not be, panels and covers back on.
Walk the customer through the fix in plain words and hand them one maintenance tip.
Photograph the finished work for your record; leave when the system is running normally.
stop_conditions: If anything looks wrong during the walkdown, you are not done: fix it now, not on a return trip.
If the customer wants changes beyond the quoted work, quote them separately instead of folding them in free.
If the system cannot reach normal operation, do not close the call as complete.

title: Build Your Diagnostic Kit in Stages, Not on Credit
mechanism_check: Airflow-first diagnosis (hvac-007) needs almost no gear; most early-career money is wasted on meters that never leave the truck.
A staged kit grows with the skills that use it: each tool earns its cost by unlocking a measurement you could not improvise.
Improvised tools are not inferior: a manometer you built (hvac-026) teaches pressure better than one you bought.
improvised_tools: Stage one: flashlight, multimeter, clamp thermometer, manometer materials from hvac-026
Stage two: combustion-free CO detector for gas homes, borescope, data-logging thermometer
A written want list ranked by calls-per-month, not by catalog gloss
steps: Start with what diagnosis already proves it needs: light, meter, temperature, improvised pressure.
Log every call where a missing tool blocked you; buy the one that appears most often first.
Keep the improvised tools working alongside the purchased ones: redundancy on a hot roof is survival.
Re-rate the want list quarterly; sell or retire tools that never leave the bag.
Budget one tool purchase per profitable month: the kit grows with the career, not ahead of it.
stop_conditions: Never buy a tool that measures something you do not yet understand: skill first, then instrument.
No tool purchase justifies cutting the parts or training budget: tools do not replace either.
If a measurement requires opening the sealed system, the missing tool is a licensed tech, not a gauge set.

title: Read the House Like a Building Scientist
mechanism_check: Comfort complaints are house problems wearing equipment masks: a hot room is often shell and duct, not capacity.
Airflow, pressure, and the building shell interact: sealing ducts (hvac-013) without knowing pressures can starve the return.
The building-scientist view combines equipment, duct, and shell into one system: you fix the right one the first time.
improvised_tools: The airflow walk (hvac-004) plus improvised manometer (hvac-026)
A window-and-door audit: where air and heat leak in plain sight
One sketch of the house with room temperatures, register flows, and shell weak spots marked
steps: Map the complaint rooms: hot, cold, humid, drafty, with temperatures and times of day.
Walk the airflow and pressures as usual, then walk the shell: attic insulation, leaky windows, garage walls, sun loads.
Mark on one sketch where duct losses, shell losses, and equipment limits each bite.
Fix in leverage order: cheapest gain first, usually sealing and airflow, then shell, equipment last.
Recheck the complaint rooms after each stage; stop spending when comfort is restored.
stop_conditions: Do not resize equipment from comfort complaints alone: that is a load calculation, not a guess.
If shell or duct work needs licensed trades or permits, scope it and hand it off.
If the house shows mold or serious air-quality issues, stop comfort work and address moisture first.

title: Climb the Ladder: Install Helper to Lead Tech
mechanism_check: The HVAC career ladder is skill-gated, not time-gated: pay follows what you can diagnose alone at 2 a.m.
Each rung has a visible proof: helper carries and watches, installer builds, service tech diagnoses, lead tech teaches and quotes.
Certifications and clean truck habits are the paper trail that makes the raise argument undeniable.
improvised_tools: A written skill map: diagnosis, electrical, gas, airflow, customer, quoting, teaching
Your call journal from hvac-039 as proof of growth
Certification targets: EPA 608 at minimum, then NATE or equivalent
steps: Name your current rung honestly and the one proof that would move you up.
Pick one skill map row per quarter and work it on every call: diagnosis discipline, electrical safety, gas sequence.
Earn EPA 608: refrigerant is the licensed line and the licensed paycheck.
Shadow a lead tech on quotes and customer conversations: that is a separate skill, not a personality trait.
Bring the skill map, the journal, and the certs to the raise conversation: evidence, not entitlement.
stop_conditions: Never fake a rung: claiming diagnostic skill you lack endangers customers and ends careers.
Do not skip the licensed line to impress: touching refrigerant without the card is a career-ending move.
If the shop never trains or promotes, the ladder continues elsewhere: loyalty goes to the craft first.

title: Run a Two-Tech Install Day: Roles, Staging, Handoffs
mechanism_check: Two techs on one install fail on handoffs, not on skill: the day dies when both assume the other ran the vacuum or wired the stat.
Clear roles beat shared everything: one owner per task means nothing is assumed done.
Staging is the invisible work: material at the attic hatch before the attic trip saves an hour of ladder climbs.
improvised_tools: Named roles for the day: equipment lead, electrical-and-controls lead, runner
A shared task board: whiteboard, tape on the truck, or phone note
A staging checklist run before the first ladder goes up
steps: Walk the job together for ten minutes: who owns indoor, who owns outdoor, who runs parts.
Stage all material, tools, and ladders before any wrench turns: nothing leaves the site mid-job.
Call handoffs out loud: 'vacuum running,' 'vacuum at 500 microns,' 'stat wired, power on.'
The controls lead verifies the other tech's wiring and vice versa: four eyes before power-up.
Commission together: startup sequence, airflow check, customer handoff done as one crew.
stop_conditions: If roles blur and both techs are in the attic while nobody watches the vacuum pump, reset roles immediately.
If a gas line or electrical panel looks wrong, both stop: the day plan yields to the hazard.
If the crew is arguing instead of handing off, pause the job ten minutes: a reset is cheaper than a mistake.

title: The Attic Dance: Two-Tech Radio Protocol Under Pressure
mechanism_check: Attic and air-handler work splits the crew by a ceiling: the person who can see the problem cannot reach the power, and vice versa.
Without a protocol, 'kill it' means different things at different breakers: ambiguity at 240 volts is how injuries happen.
A fixed call-and-response removes ambiguity under heat, noise, and attic disorientation.
improvised_tools: Two phones on speaker or cheap radios
A fixed vocabulary: ready, kill it, safe to touch, stand clear, say again
A rule: the hands-off tech owns the power, the hands-on tech never touches live
steps: Agree the vocabulary before anyone climbs: no synonyms, no shortcuts.
Hands-on tech narrates what they are about to touch; hands-off tech confirms power state first.
Power changes follow call-and-response: 'ready to kill the disconnect,' 'disconnect killed,' 'safe to touch.'
If a word is missed, the only legal response is 'say again': never assume.
Debrief at the truck: where did the protocol strain, and what changes next time.
stop_conditions: If communication drops, the hands-on tech goes hands-off immediately until it is restored.
If anyone says 'stop,' everything stops: no context required, no debate.
If the attic heat is causing dizziness or confusion, both techs descend: heat illness is not a communication problem.

title: The Twenty-Minute Skill Swap: Train Each Other Weekly
mechanism_check: Crews learn faster than individuals: one tech's hard-won lesson becomes everyone's if there is a ritual to transfer it.
The weekly swap is that ritual: twenty minutes, one topic, one demonstration, zero slides.
Teaching is the teacher's upgrade too: the one who explains a fault path this week diagnoses it faster next week.
improvised_tools: One standing weekly slot, same time, shop or tailgate
A topic rotation list anyone can add to
A broken or retired part to pass around and dissect
steps: Rotate who teaches each week; the newest tech teaches at least as often as the oldest.
One topic only: one diagnosis, one fix, one habit.
Demonstrate on real hardware: a failed capacitor, a clogged trap, a seized contactor.
Everyone states one thing they will do differently on their next call.
Write the topic and the takeaway on the rotation list for the next crew to find.
stop_conditions: If the swap becomes a lecture with no hands on the part, end it: demonstration or nothing.
If attendance is mandatory but nobody teaches, kill the ritual and rebuild it around volunteers.
If the topic touches the licensed line, frame it as diagnose-to-the-line: teach the boundary, not the breach.

title: Heat-Wave Surge: Triage the Call Board as a Crew
mechanism_check: A heat wave turns the call board into triage: every customer is urgent, but the crew's hours are fixed.
Triage sorts by consequence, not by who called first: no-cool for elderly and infants outranks mild underperformance.
A crew that triages together stays sane; one that first-come-first-serves burns out by day three.
improvised_tools: One visible call board, sorted by consequence, owned by the dispatcher or lead
A phone-triage script: two questions that sort the board without a truck roll
A cooling-center list for the truly vulnerable: know it before the wave hits
steps: Score each call on consequence: vulnerable occupants, medical equipment, total failure vs degraded.
Phone-triage the low scores first: thermostat reset and filter checks resolve calls that never needed a truck.
Batch geographically: the crew runs zones, not zigzags, and the board updates after every call.
Rotate the brutal calls: attics and rooftops shared, not dumped on the junior tech.
End of day, re-score the board for tomorrow: heat waves move, triage moves with them.
stop_conditions: If the board outruns the crew's hours, tell dispatch and the customers honestly: overpromising is its own failure.
If techs are showing heat illness or exhaustion, pull them: a sick tech helps no one.
If a call involves gas smell or electrical burning, it jumps the board and gets the fastest response.

title: Apprentice Leads, Journeyman Watches: Graduated Responsibility
mechanism_check: Apprentices plateau when they only assist: judgment grows only when the decision is theirs to make.
Graduated responsibility hands the call to the apprentice in stages, with the journeyman as a safety net, not a supervisor standing over the shoulder.
The mechanism is trust with a boundary: the apprentice owns everything up to the licensed and gas lines, which stay with the mentor.
improvised_tools: A three-stage ladder: narrate, then lead with mentor present, then lead with mentor on call
The hypothesis rule from hvac-039: apprentice states it before tools come out
A debrief sheet: what the apprentice decided, what worked, what to change
steps: Stage one: apprentice narrates the mentor's diagnosis aloud, naming each test and why.
Stage two: apprentice runs the call with the mentor present and silent unless a stop condition appears.
Stage three: apprentice runs the call alone with the mentor one phone call away.
Move up a stage only after three clean calls at the current stage: clean means no stop-condition rescues.
Debrief every call at the truck: the apprentice speaks first about what they would change.
stop_conditions: The mentor reclaims the call instantly at any gas smell, electrical doubt, or licensed-line boundary: no negotiation.
If the apprentice hides a mistake, they drop back a stage: hiding is the failure, not the mistake.
If the customer is uncomfortable with the apprentice leading, the mentor leads: trust is earned, not assigned.
